analysis.one_liner: Gives middle-income families a refundable tax credit for wartime cost increases and bans price gouging on fuel and essentials during the conflict.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by a single representative with no cosponsors and referred to two House committees, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill responds to higher energy, grocery, and commuting costs tied to the U.S.-Israel-Iran conflict. It creates a temporary, refundable tax credit for households earning between $80,000 and $160,000, sized by the Treasury Department to offset war-related increases in living costs. It also makes it an unlawful deceptive practice, enforceable by the FTC and the Justice Department, for sellers of fuel, heating fuels, and essential goods to charge prices that are grossly higher than before the conflict without a cost-based justification. All of its provisions expire when the war-related energy emergency ends.
analysis.who_benefits: Middle-income households earning $80,000 to $160,000 a year — families often too well-off for low-income assistance but without savings to absorb a sustained price shock [S2]. They would receive a refundable tax credit covering commuting, grocery, and utility increases tied to the war, adjusted for family size and regional costs [S2]. All consumers would also gain protection against unjustified wartime price increases on gasoline, heating fuel, electricity, food, and basic household goods, with restitution available through Justice Department suits and state gouging laws left intact [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable tax credit for households earning between $80,000 and $160,000, with the amount calculated by the Treasury Department to offset war-related increases in commuting, grocery, and utility costs, adjusted for family size and regional cost differences.

Makes it an unfair or deceptive practice, under the Federal Trade Commission Act, for any wholesale or retail seller of motor fuel, heating fuels, electricity, or essential consumer staples to charge a grossly excessive price increase over pre-conflict levels that is not substantially attributable to real costs incurred.

Gives both the FTC and the Justice Department enforcement authority, including civil penalties and restitution for affected consumers, and explicitly preserves state price-gouging laws and state attorney general enforcement.

Requires the FTC to study how state and local price-gouging laws performed during the conflict and to recommend whether a permanent federal baseline standard is warranted, a record that outlasts the bill's own sunset.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and fuel sellers whose wartime price increases cannot be justified by actual costs, since they would face FTC and Justice Department enforcement, civil penalties, and restitution [S2]. Retailers of food and basic household goods would face the same prohibition on unjustified price hikes [S2]. Federal taxpayers would fund the refundable credit, which has no stated dollar cap in the bill text — the amount is left entirely to Treasury's calculation [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Fuel and staple sellers; federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The credit has no defined dollar amount: the bill leaves it to the Treasury Secretary to 'reasonably calculate' the offset, so the actual benefit families would receive is unknown and could change with each administration's interpretation.

A federal prohibition on 'grossly excessive' price increases can suppress supply incentives at the worst moment: sellers who fear enforcement may hold back output or redirect fuel elsewhere, which can worsen shortages during a real supply disruption.

The credit covers only households between $80,000 and $160,000; lower-income families facing the same higher gasoline, heating, and grocery bills are excluded from this particular relief, though they may qualify for other programs.

Defining 'grossly excessive' is left largely to FTC rulemaking, and the price benchmark is a 60-day pre-enactment average, which could penalize sellers whose costs rose for reasons the record cannot cleanly separate from the war.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the families it targets, the bill offers concrete relief during a genuine cost shock, and the anti-gouging provision has a real enforcement structure with restitution for consumers rather than being symbolic. The strongest honest objection is economic: price controls during a supply disruption carry a real risk of aggravating shortages, and the vaguely defined credit gives the Treasury Department enormous discretion with no fiscal ceiling. The bill's narrow income band and its sunset provision limit both its cost and its reach.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced by one representative, referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, and has seen no hearings, markup, or floor action; the current Congress is still in session, so its fate is not yet sealed.

narrative.text: Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick (D-FL) introduced the bill on April 9, 2026, with no cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, splitting its tax provisions from its consumer-protection provisions between two committees.
No further action — no hearing, markup, vote, or floor consideration — appears in the bill's action history after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo: energy producers and sellers keep wartime pricing free of federal anti-gouging enforcement, and middle-income families receive no targeted relief. Because Congress is still in session, nothing has been finally decided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, the status quo holds

for.name: Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick
for.what_they_did: Introduced the W.A.R. Act, providing a wartime middle-income tax credit and a federal price-gouging prohibition, and secured its referral to two committees.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred and no opposition has been recorded; the bill has zero cosponsors and no committee action, so no partisan pattern has formed yet.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and fuel retailers
industries.note: The bill's anti-gouging prohibition directly targets motor fuel, diesel, and heating fuel sellers, exposing them to FTC and Justice Department enforcement, penalties, and restitution when wartime price increases exceed documented costs. Its interest in keeping wartime windfall pricing unregulated runs against consumers paying at the pump.

Sellers of food and basic household necessities would face the same prohibition on grossly excessive, cost-unjustified price increases. Chains whose margins stay tied to actual costs would see little change, while those raising prices beyond costs during the emergency would bear enforcement risk.

Taxpayers fund the refundable credit, which has no stated dollar cap, with the total cost depending on Treasury's calculation and how long the conflict-related emergency lasts. The credit is temporary by design and terminates when the emergency ends.

analysis.trajectory: This bill faces long odds. It has no cosponsors, and tax measures plus consumer-protection measures split jurisdiction between the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, each of which can slow it independently. First-term-cycle bills with a single sponsor and no committee action this far into a session rarely reach the floor; unless the sponsor attracts cosponsors or the committees schedule hearings, it will likely die quietly when this Congress ends in January 2027.
